RESULT v1 | k41649c01a6 | When two members of a Raft cluster lose connectivity (a network partition), the cluster immediately splits into a majority side and a minority side. Only the side that still holds a quorum of voters (majority of the original cluster membership) can elect a leader or commit new entries; the minority side, even if it contains a leader with uncommitted entries, stops committing and cannot serve linearizable writes. Its pending client operations hang or fail. On the majority side, the leader keeps appending new commands to its write-ahead log and replicating them to a quorum — and because the log-compaction (snapshotting) interval is unconstrained (never triggered), nothing ever checkpoint-truncates the log. The log grows monotonically, consuming disk, until the disk fills and the node (and eventually the whole majority quorum) cannot persist entries. Writes now fail even on the quorum side, so the cluster becomes effectively unavailable — the partition converts a transient split-brain into permanent-looking downtime, with the minority side holding divergent, stale log tails that were never snapshotted.  Upon reinnection, divergence is resolved by Raft's deterministic conflict-resolution strategy: log matching by (term, index) precedence, i.e., leader-forced overwrite with follower truncation. Every replicated entry carries its leader's term and its position in the unified log. When the healed majority leader sends AppendEntries to a partition-reconnected follower, the follower's consistency check (prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm for prior terms) plus leaderLastIndex for its current term causes the follower to replace any entries that conflict with the leader's and delete all entries beyond the replicated leader's last index. A higher-term follower that briefly led the minority side steps down because the healed leader has the same or higher current term. Commit progresses only once an entry is replicated on a majority of the current configuration. Uncommitted minority-side proposals are discarded via this truncation.  One explicit tradeoff: Raft deliberately sacrifices availability to preserve consistency — during the partition (and while the bloated log blocks a snapshot), no data is written and minority-side data is lost, instead of risking divergent states being committed on both sides. A second real-world tradeoff is that choosing an unconstrained (rare/never) snapshot interval saves the CPU and I/O cost of snapshotting, but it allows unbounded log growth and stalls commit progress exactly when recovery after a partition is most needed.  Success criteria addressed: the conflict-resolution strategy is named — log truncation with leader-forced log overwrite by (term, index) precedence, discarding uncommitted entries — and a tradeoff is identified — availability sacrificed for consistency during the partition (and unbounded-growth/snapshot-overhead tradeoff).
